## 4. Landing

A batch lands its commits on the integration branch it was given, which is never checked
out. Before committing, the diff is checked to contain no unrelated work. A commit carries
no trailer but the co-author trailers of the campaign's [identity](#6-identity), and its
subject says what it does and which run made it. A batch's names its module's file and its
objective and ends with its run's id, as `refs.c: wrap 12 items (wave-3/batch-1/run-2)`,
and its body lists the items it translated by their anchors' paths, as
`fn::git_reference_lookup`, one per line; a review batch's two commits name what they file
and what they fix the same way, and a planner run's subject ends with its run's id. A
progress commit is `progress: wave-<index>`, and an integration's merge, in the campaign's
repository and on the fork's `main`, `integrate <module>`, the module written as
[`modules-schema`](../../artifacts/modules-schema/SKILL.md) writes it.

The landing operation is a local push of the batch's tip to the integration branch through
the repository's Git common directory, which accepts only a fast-forward. A direct ref
update is no substitute: its compare-and-swap form makes the update atomic, but does not
enforce that the new commit descends from the expected old commit.

### 4.1 The landing lock

An integration branch is landed on by one batch at a time, under its landing lock: an
exclusive `flock` on a file in the Git common directory, named after the branch with its
`refs/heads/` prefix dropped, so that every worktree of the repository sees the same lock:

```text
$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/crustify/landing/<integration branch>.lock
```

A batch whose validated work is committed on its own branch takes the lock and holds it
until its landing has succeeded:

1. it acquires the lock, waiting while another batch holds it;
2. it rebases only its own branch onto the current integration branch, once: nothing else
   lands while it holds the lock;
3. it resolves any conflict the rebase raises and runs again, on the rebased tree, the
   gates that could catch a regression of the integration, as
   [`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section describes, fixing what fails;
4. it pushes the fast-forward, which nothing can reject; and
5. it releases the lock.

A conflict or a failing gate is resolved under the lock rather than after releasing it, so
that the branch cannot move again in between and no batch rebases twice.

The waiter blocks in `flock` itself, so the kernel wakes it the moment the lock is released,
and nothing polls. Once it holds the lock, it hands the locked descriptor to a process of
its own, detached from the shell that started it and bound to the lifetime of the agent's
CLI: a `flock` lock belongs to the open file, so that process keeps it after the command
that took it exits, until that CLI ends, however it ends, and the kernel releases it. The
holder records itself beside the lock, in `<integration branch>.lock.holder`, as its own pid
and the CLI's. A waiter bounds each wait, to stay within the time a single command may run,
and waits again when it expires. For example, with `$CLI_PID` the agent CLI's pid, found by
walking up the shell's parent processes:
<!-- TODO: this procedure must run exactly so: it belongs in a script beside this skill,
documented by its `--help`, as `authoring` describes. -->

```bash
lock="$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/crustify/landing/<integration branch>.lock"
mkdir -p "$(dirname "$lock")"
# wait in the kernel, up to 10 minutes per command; then hand the lock to a detached holder
sh -c '
  exec 9>"$1"
  flock -w 600 9 || exit 1
  setsid sh -c "echo \"\$\$ $2\" > \"$1.holder\"; exec tail --pid=$2 -f /dev/null" 9>&9 &
' sh "$lock" "$CLI_PID"
# release, once the push has succeeded
holder=$(cut -d' ' -f1 "$lock.holder"); rm -f "$lock.holder"; kill "$holder"
```

The holder file is removed before the holder is ended, while the lock is still held, so
that a release never removes the next holder's record.

The lock has no timeout: the regression gates it covers vary in length. A holder that has
stopped making progress keeps it until its agent is ended. That releases it where the
agent ran in a CLI of its own. An agent that shared its CLI with others leaves its holder
running: the holder is then ended as a release ends it, by the pid its record names, the
record removed first. The batch is then run again, as any failed batch is.

### 4.2 Commits

Every landing is a fast-forward, so an integration branch is linear, and each batch's
commits are one unbroken run of it, ending at its branch's tip and starting after the wave
base or the tip of the batch that landed before it: the commits its branch reaches and
neither the wave base nor the wave's other landed batches reach, oldest first, which
become the batch's `commits` in `schedule.json`.

The integration branch is never reset, force-updated or moved backward, and nothing is
pushed to a remote. The worktree stays after landing, until it is purged as [Lifecycle](#5-lifecycle)
describes.
<!-- TODO: when the working and shipping branches, and a wrapper's, are pushed to their
remotes is not specified yet, though a wrapper's reuse and a Git-pinned dependency need
it. -->

### 4.3 Promotion

### 5.5 Batches

A batch's branch and worktree, forked from its wave branch's tip, are created before it
launches, with its run dir, as [`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md) describes. The gitignored state its tree needs and does
not build itself, such as shared analysis databases, is symlinked from the base checkout,
and its `c/` is a worktree of the base checkout's submodule at the commit the superproject
records, since no batch changes the C.
Once the batch has landed, its worktree is purged; its branch stays until its commits are
recorded in `schedule.json`, since they are derived from it, as
[Landing](#4-landing) describes. A batch that fails keeps its branch and worktree for
inspection; they are removed before it is run again, which forks them anew.

## 6. Identity

Every commit of a campaign, in its repository and its wrappers', is authored and committed
as Crustify, whose GitHub account is `crustify-ai` and whose git identity is
`crustify <crustify@berkeley.edu>`, whatever the repository's git configuration says,
unless the settings' `identity` answer names another: an author and any co-authors, each
as `Name <email>`. The author named there then authors and commits every commit, and each
message ends with one `Co-Authored-By:` trailer per co-author and no other, none that an
agent's host suggests included.

The identity is passed explicitly, as configuration on the command line, to every command
that writes a commit, a rebase, a merge and a cherry-pick as much as a commit, since the
host may have no git identity of its own.

```text
$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/crustify/landing/<integration branch>.lock
```

A batch whose validated work is committed on its own branch takes the lock and holds it
until its landing has succeeded:

1. it acquires the lock, waiting while another batch holds it;
2. it rebases only its own branch onto the current integration branch, once: nothing else
   lands while it holds the lock;
3. it resolves any conflict the rebase raises and runs again, on the rebased tree, the
   gates that could catch a regression of the integration, as
   [`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section describes, fixing what fails;
4. it pushes the fast-forward, which nothing can reject; and
5. it releases the lock.

A conflict or a failing gate is resolved under the lock rather than after releasing it, so
that the branch cannot move again in between and no batch rebases twice.

The waiter blocks in `flock` itself, so the kernel wakes it the moment the lock is released,
and nothing polls. Once it holds the lock, it hands the locked descriptor to a process of
its own, detached from the shell that started it and bound to the lifetime of the agent's
CLI: a `flock` lock belongs to the open file, so that process keeps it after the command
that took it exits, until that CLI ends, however it ends, and the kernel releases it. The
holder records itself beside the lock, in `<integration branch>.lock.holder`, as its own pid
and the CLI's. A waiter bounds each wait, to stay within the time a single command may run,
and waits again when it expires. For example, with `$CLI_PID` the agent CLI's pid, found by
walking up the shell's parent processes:
<!-- TODO: this procedure must run exactly so: it belongs in a script beside this skill,
documented by its `--help`, as `authoring` describes. -->

```bash
lock="$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/crustify/landing/<integration branch>.lock"
mkdir -p "$(dirname "$lock")"
# wait in the kernel, up to 10 minutes per command; then hand the lock to a detached holder
sh -c '
  exec 9>"$1"
  flock -w 600 9 || exit 1
  setsid sh -c "echo \"\$\$ $2\" > \"$1.holder\"; exec tail --pid=$2 -f /dev/null" 9>&9 &
' sh "$lock" "$CLI_PID"
# release, once the push has succeeded
holder=$(cut -d' ' -f1 "$lock.holder"); rm -f "$lock.holder"; kill "$holder"
```

The holder file is removed before the holder is ended, while the lock is still held, so
that a release never removes the next holder's record.

The lock has no timeout: the regression gates it covers vary in length. A holder that has
stopped making progress keeps it until its agent is ended. That releases it where the
agent ran in a CLI of its own. An agent that shared its CLI with others leaves its holder
running: the holder is then ended as a release ends it, by the pid its record names, the
record removed first. The batch is then run again, as any failed batch is.

### 4.2 Commits

Every landing is a fast-forward, so an integration branch is linear, and each batch's
commits are one unbroken run of it, ending at its branch's tip and starting after the wave
base or the tip of the batch that landed before it: the commits its branch reaches and
neither the wave base nor the wave's other landed batches reach, oldest first, which
become the batch's `commits` in `schedule.json`.

The integration branch is never reset, force-updated or moved backward, and nothing is
pushed to a remote. The worktree stays after landing, until it is purged as [Lifecycle](#5-lifecycle)
describes.

### 4.3 Promotion

### 5.5 Batches

A batch's branch and worktree, forked from its wave branch's tip, are created before it
launches, with its run dir, as [`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md) describes. The gitignored state its tree needs and does
not build itself, such as shared analysis databases, is symlinked from the base checkout,
and its `c/` is a worktree of the base checkout's submodule at the commit the superproject
records, since no batch changes the C.
Once the batch has landed, its worktree is purged; its branch stays until its commits are
recorded in `schedule.json`, since they are derived from it, as
[Landing](#4-landing) describes. A batch that fails keeps its branch and worktree for
inspection; they are removed before it is run again, which forks them anew.

Every commit of a campaign, in its repository and its wrappers', is authored and committed

//! `deps/llhttp/api.c`: llhttp's public API over its generated parser, ported to Rust.
2505 src/libgit2/deps/llhttp/llhttp.rs
api.rs
http.rs
llhttp.rs
# A callback whose context is reached through an argument has no sound C form

Status: `open`.

## Signal

Skills that leave a case unspecified that a binding cannot settle well (`evolution` §2).
`binding-symbols`' Function pointers section builds a callable type's C half from "a C
function, with its context, which Rust calls … through an `unsafe` constructor whose
contract states … its context's lifetime and threads, and safe to call". For a function
pointer "without a context parameter" it says the Rust half carries no captured state. It
does not cover the case where C has no context parameter because the context lives in an
argument: there the C function's soundness depends on the argument, not on anything the
callable type holds, so a safe `call` with an arbitrary argument cannot be sound.

## Evidence

`wave-194/batch-1/run-1`: `llhttp_cb` (`int (*)(llhttp_t *)`) and `llhttp_data_cb` take no
context; their context is the parser's `data`, which libgit2's C callbacks
(`transports/httpclient.c`'s `on_header_field`, `on_body`, …) read as an
`http_parser_context *`. The batch's `Callback::from_fn` (`pub(crate)`) can only require
that the function be sound "with every live, exclusively held parser, whatever its `data`
and `settings` hold", which no such C callback meets: `Callback::call(Parser::new()…)`

Status: `open`.

## Signal

A rule the how-to skills lack, which a binding had to work out by hand (`evolution` §2).

parsed, so a Rust handler receives that parser's exclusive handle, from which a safe API

### `libgit2/deps/llhttp/api.c` wave 194 batch 0: `llhttp.c`'s types ahead of api.c

A wrap batch ahead of its consumer: `deps/llhttp/llhttp.c`'s five types, which api.c's
`port` waves use, bound in llhttp.c's own file, `src/libgit2/deps/llhttp/llhttp.rs`, which
its wave 238 ports. `st::llhttp__internal_s` is `Parser`, a `define_ctype!` layout with
`ParserRef` and `ParserMut`, and its typedefs `llhttp__internal_t`, `llhttp_t` and
`git_http_parser` are the aliases `InternalT`, `LlhttpT` and `HttpParser`. A parser owns
nothing and C keeps no pointer to one, so it is a plain value: `CZeroable`, with no owner or
policy; its constructor, `llhttp__internal_init` through `llhttp_init`, is the next batch's.
The closed enums `llhttp_errno`, `llhttp_method`, `llhttp_status` and `llhttp_type` are
`Errno`, `Method`, `Status` and `ParserType`, 185 variants over bindgen's constants with
fallible conversions and an `Unnamed*` error each, their typedefs aliases (`ErrnoT`, …).

The `fields` cell counts the 21 assigned. 15 have accessors: the fields api.c, http.c,
`transports/httpclient.c` and `transports/httpparser.c` touch. The other six, `_index`,
`_span_pos0`, `_span_cb0`, `_current`, `header_state` and `initial_message_completed`, only
llhttp.c's generated code reads or writes (`query structs --field-touchers`), and three of
them would send it through a wild pointer or out of a table if written from outside, so they
have none (`crustify/evolution/wrap-ahead-field-users`). The fields holding an enum's value
are read typed and fallibly, and raw (`*_raw`) as api.c's getters return them; the flag words
and `finish` raw, until `llhttp_flags`, `llhttp_lenient_flags` and `llhttp_finish` are bound.
`reason` is lent as a `&CStr` for the handle's borrow and set only from a `&'static CStr`;
`error_pos` is never followed, only compared with a caller's slice (`error_offset`); `data`
and `settings` are read as addresses and set through the batch's two `unsafe fn`s, whose
contracts carry what the callbacks read through them. Those four are the boundary scan's
sites in the changeset: no safe form replaces a user's untyped context, and `settings`'
typed getter waits for `llhttp_settings_s`, api.c's item, which the cycle through
`llhttp_cb` puts after this batch (T3 drops the cast edge). The pointer findings of the
struct's eight pointer fields, and `llhttp__internal_init`'s and `llhttp_init`'s `init`
roles, are in the ownership store.

The raw bindings gain `llhttp.h` in `wrapper.h`, the five types with their typedefs, and
api.c's `llhttp_init`, `llhttp_settings_init`, `llhttp_execute` and nine getters, which the
equivalence tests compare with; `llhttp_settings_s` and the callback typedefs come in with
them. Tests: 12 `unit_pub` (the enums' values and errors, every setter against its getter),
4 `ub_safe` (reborrows, a lent reason, parsers moved in a `Vec`), 6 `ub_unsafe` (one suite
per `unsafe` setter: callbacks reading the stored context through C, a context replaced
between calls, NULL settings, a table that ignores `data`), 8 `equiv` (two parsers fed the
same input by `llhttp_execute`, one read through api.c's getters and one through the
handles, compared after every step: a response in pieces, an unnamed status, requests with
their method and upgrade, an invalid message, a callback's own error, a pause and resume, the
lenient flags, the setters' effect on the C) and 5 compile-fail doctests. llhttp has no C
tests of its own in the tree.

Coverage was measured with `crustify/scripts/coverage/run.sh` on a `git archive` of the wave
tip `2216b0cd0` and on this tree, each suite alone, and read with `report.py` from the
scratch tree's `src/libgit2`, the unit column merging `lib` and `unit_pub`. The tip's Rust
figures are the recorded ones; its C figures read `27.92`% (`ub_safe`), `19.08`%
(`ub_unsafe`), `42.51`% (`equiv`), `31.37`% (unit) and `44.98`% (total), against which the pp
cells are taken. The C total moves
by `+1.12` pp: the equivalence and unsafe-setter tests run llhttp's parser, which nothing
reached before (`llhttp.c` 18.64% of lines, `http.c` 78.35%, `api.c` 11.99%). Worklist:
`llhttp.rs` 110 of 110 lines, 33 of 33 functions, 147 of 148 regions; the region missed,
`error_offset`'s return for a position before the slice, has an assertion added after the
measurement. Of the parser's states the tests reach the initialised, parsing, paused,
upgrade-paused and failed ones, and the transitions between them that the setters and
`llhttp_execute` make. The Overview's Rust LoC moves by ffimap's `code.loc.total` (`+919`)
and `code.tests.loc.total` (`+683`); `wrapped types` counts the five against the recorded
`258`.

The safety audit scans (ffimap `9aa2ef1`, `--ffibox`, `--sys-crates pcre2_sys`, the 13 seams,
`--regions ffi_import,ffi_export`): `pub raw ptr`, `pub void ptr` and `pub unsafe fn` are the
two getters and two setters above, `raw→std` the reason's `CStr::from_ptr`, `C by value`
three mentions of `llhttp__internal_s` by value in the layout and its handles' seams, and the
raw derefs and unsafe blocks the accessors' one-operation projections and reads. The four
`unsafe` blocks the first scan found outside the regions were the `Unnamed*` errors' `write!`
(std's `format_args!`, which ffimap counts); their `Display` writes its parts instead, as
`basics.rs`'s `UnnamedHashId` does. `ffimap api` against the tip: the five items are `new`, as
are all 212 anchor keys of the file (the 185 constants, 15 fields and 7 typedefs with them),
and every unattributed module is `kept` but the raw `sys::libgit2`, `extended`.

Gates, on the base `2216b0cd0`, the wave branch's tip when the batch landed: the workspace is
formatted, and `clippy --all-targets` passes with warnings denied on `plain`. The whole
workspace passes on `plain` (`lib` 840 and 1 ignored, `ub_safe` 766, `ub_unsafe` 126,
`equiv` 536, `unit_pub` 79, `hidden_symbols` 1, doctests 72 merged and 383 standalone). The
batch's tests pass under ASan+UBSan, and its `unit_pub` and `ub_safe` tests under Miri; each
`equiv` and `ub_unsafe` test was run alone there and stops at `llhttp_init` or
`llhttp_settings_init` (`calls C`). TSan has no obligation: no `Send` or `Sync` is asserted
and no thread added; nor has BSan, which nothing here is expected to trigger. The package
builds alone in bundled mode, with `glibc-bindings` and `ffibox` patched to their local
sources and CMake and pkg-config given the side campaigns' `plain` installs of OpenSSL, PCRE2
and zlib. Usage cells are the assistant's.

### `libgit2/deps/llhttp/api.c` wave 194 batch 1: `llhttp.c`'s parse, callbacks and X-macros ahead of api.c

The second wrap batch ahead of api.c's ports: `deps/llhttp/llhttp.c`'s seven symbols, in
`src/libgit2/deps/llhttp/llhttp.rs`. `fn::llhttp__internal_init` is `Parser::new` (and
`Default`), the safe constructor batch 0 left, and `ParserMut::reinit` in place, which
`llhttp_init` and `llhttp_reset` start from; its `init` role in the ownership store holds
against its body (`memset`, then the start state). `fn::llhttp__internal_execute` is
`ParserMut::parse(&[u8]) -> Result<Parsed, ParseError>`, the run's start and end one slice:
`HPE_OK` and the two resumable pauses are `Parsed`, since libgit2's `httpparser.c` treats
them as an early stop, and any other code, an `llhttp_errno` or a data callback's own value,
is a `ParseError` the parser keeps. The names leave api.c's own (`init`, `reset`,
`execute`) to its port. Two C behaviours are refused rather than carried: a parser with no
state to run from (`_current` is `s_error`, 0, with no error, as `Parser::zeroed()` or a
parser cleared after `HPE_PAUSED_H2_UPGRADE` leaves it) reaches `abort()`, and a callback
that executes or initialises the parser whose execute runs it corrupts the outer run (a span
pointing into the nested input, `_index` past a match sequence). `parse` panics on the
first, and `parse` and `reinit` on the second through a thread-local register of the parsers
each thread is executing, which the trampolines' barrier turns into the callback's error
(`crustify/evolution/callback-reenters-its-caller`).

`fnp::llhttp_cb` and `fnp::llhttp_data_cb` are `Callback` and `DataCallback`, a function
pointer each, `Copy` and never released: neither has a context parameter, the parser's
`data` being the context, so a Rust implementation is a stateless `EventHandler` or
`DataHandler` type reached through a trampoline behind `callback::barrier` (`-1` on a panic,
a NULL parser or a NULL run), as `trace.rs`'s `git_trace_cb` is. The C form is a
`pub(crate)` `unsafe` constructor, whose contract no C callback that reads `data` meets;
such a callback is reached through the settings its parser runs with
(`crustify/evolution/callback-context-in-an-argument`). `call` is safe, and `raw` gives the
slot value a settings table holds, which api.c's `llhttp_settings_s` binds next.
`mac::HTTP_ERRNO_MAP`, `mac::HTTP_ALL_METHOD_MAP` and `mac::HTTP_STATUS_MAP` are the enums'
own tables, not a second one: their entries are batch 0's variants in the enums' order,
which the X-macros share. Each of `Errno`, `Method` and `Status` gains `MAP`, `map_name`
(`NAME`), `map_string` (`STRING`) and `constant_name` (`PREFIX##NAME`, the case label, and
`llhttp_errno_name`'s text), each a `&'static CStr` sliced at compile time from the
stringified bindgen constant; `llhttp_enum!` takes the one `STRING` that differs,
`M-SEARCH`, beside its variant, and checks every prefix at compile time. They are
`Replaces`, so the three count as ported symbols, the four others as wrapped.

The raw bindings gain the two functions, the two callback types and, for the equivalence
tests, api.c's `llhttp_errno_name`, `llhttp_method_name` and `llhttp_status_name`. The
ownership store gains the pointer findings of `llhttp__internal_execute` (the run's
pointers retained in `_span_pos0` and `error_pos` and never followed after the call) and of
the two callback types. Tests: 17 `unit_pub` (the maps' columns and order, the parse in
every run size, pauses, upgrade, the kept error, the two panics, the callbacks and their
panics), 7 `ub_safe` (runs freed between parses, parsers moved mid-message, runs at the
edges of their allocations, handlers called from Rust that parse and initialise, callbacks

against `llhttp__internal_init`, private state included; `parse` against

doctests and 2 compile-fail doctests (a handler sending its parser to another thread, a
callable built from a bare C function). llhttp has no C tests in the tree.

---
name: conventions
description: "Naming, tree layout, anchors and test placement of the Rust a campaign generates. Read before writing, homing or reviewing generated Rust or tests."
---

# Crustify coding conventions

These are the shared, mechanical contracts of the code a campaign generates: how it is
named, where it sits, how it records what it translated and where its tests go. The
toolchain, edition, lints and formatting it is held to are [`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. Naming

The workspace's lints enforce the standard Rust casing below, as [`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s
Lints section describes.

The safe surface uses ordinary Rust naming: `snake_case` for functions, methods and
modules, `UpperCamelCase` for types and traits, `SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE` for constants and
statics. A C name's library or owning-type prefix is dropped wherever the crate, module or
receiver already supplies it, and the idiomatic Rust term is preferred over a
transliterated C one. The filled anchor records the C name, so renaming costs no
traceability. Names that cross the language boundary keep their C-derived spelling, as
below.

### 1.1 Functions

A C function's raw binding is `sys::<name>`. Its safe wrapper is a free function homed in
the owning module, named by the rules above. When one C function has several valid
ownership contracts, each safe variant has a distinct, descriptive name.

### 1.2 Types

A wrapped C type is the layout-compatible newtype `Foo`, named by the rules above; its
shared and exclusive borrowed handles are `FooRef<'a>` and `FooMut<'a>`, and its sole and
counted owners `FooBox` and `FooArc`. A port keeps these names while what they name
changes, as [`porting-types`](../porting/types/SKILL.md)'s Structs section describes. A typedef that
names a type under another name, which its item lists among its `typedefs`, is a
`pub type` alias of the type's Rust form.

A function pointer a typedef declares is named after its typedef. One written inline is
named after the site that declares it, its holder's name followed by its own and `Fn`: a
field's `<Struct><Field>Fn`, a parameter's `<Function><Param>Fn`, a return's
`<Function>ReturnFn` and a global's `<Global>Fn`.

### 1.3 Shims

A callable macro shim is `crustify_<NAME>`.

### 1.4 Exports

Each ported module has one raw ABI gateway, its `ffi_export` region, as
[Unsafe regions](#21-unsafe-regions) describes, whose exports use `#[unsafe(no_mangle)] extern "C"` under the bare C names: the
module's functions and globals that C outside the module references, another module's TU
or a C test or executable that stays, the `static inline` functions its headers define
included. The exports serve that C, which reaches the module through them once it has
switched. A function or global only the module's own C references is not exported: that
C leaves the build with the module at its switch, and its callers are Rust from then
on; nor are static functions and static globals, which nothing outside their TU reaches.
The target's public C API, for C outside the target, is deferred: exports serve the
target's own remaining C alone, and that API is a layer of its own over the native Rust API,
added once the modules it covers are ported.
<!-- TODO: that layer, a C-compatible ABI over the ported public API, is not specified
yet. Until it is, a C consumer outside the target does not survive a port. -->
An export is removed, with the raw binding that reaches it, by its symbol's `port/unexport`,
after the switch that removes the last C that calls it, takes its address or
accesses it. A C test tied to the module that stays, using only its public API, does not
hold an export back: it checks the export while other C needs it, and leaves with it.

### 1.5 Export features

Each module's `ffi_export` is compiled only under the safe crate's Cargo feature
`ffi-export-<tu>`, with `<tu>` its translation unit's path below the C root, every character
that is not an ASCII letter or digit replaced by `-`. The feature is off until the module
switches, so that its exports never collide with the C they replace, and the switch
deletes it, its gateway compiling unconditionally from then on.

## 2. Crates, modules, and TUs

The Rust tree is the repository's own, as [`layout`](../../operations/layout/SKILL.md)'s Tree section lays it
out, all relative to the repository's root:

- `Cargo.toml` - the safe crate's manifest, which also declares the workspace.
- `src/lib.rs` - the safe crate's root, with one `cfg`-gated module per link unit.
- `src/<link-unit>/` - one sub-dir per link unit.
- `src/sys.rs` and `sys/<link-unit>/` - the raw bindings, one public module per link unit,
  laid out as [`bindgen`](../bindgen/SKILL.md) describes.

The safe crate is named after its repository, `<repo>-crustify`, as
[`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Repositories section names it:
a name crates.io leaves free, which tells it apart from the source's own Rust bindings,
such as `git2` for libgit2.

Within a link unit's sub-dir, the tree follows the module decomposition in `modules.json`
exactly, and preserves the C layout as far as the idiomatic organization of a Rust tree
allows:

- each module is one `.rs` file, at its translation unit's path below the C root with the
  `.rs` extension: its TU and the headers bundled with it have no files of their own,
  since Rust has no headers;
- a header module is one `<stem>_h.rs` file, at its header's path;
- the two modules of a split foundational TU share the TU's file;
- C directories become Rust modules: a directory's `.rs` file sits beside the directory,
  as `<dir>.rs` and `<dir>/`, and declares the modules within it, or is the module of a TU
  with the directory's name where there is one; `mod.rs` files are not used; and
- a file or directory name that is not a Rust identifier is sanitized, hyphens to
  underscores, and a Rust keyword takes a trailing underscore.

Where a C layout has no idiomatic Rust counterpart, the tree adapts it in the conventional
Rust way and keeps the C path recognizable. A batch names the `.rs` file each of its items
belongs in, as `src/<link-unit>/…/<file>.rs`. Entities sharing a
definition site co-home. A home may be shared across waves.

### 2.1 Unsafe regions

A module's unsafe code is confined to at most two inline child modules of its file, its
unsafe regions, so that the rest of the file, its native code, holds none:

- `mod ffi_import`: what the module reaches in C: its calls through the raw bindings, the C
  layouts it wraps with their handles and accessors, the owners and lifecycle policies over
  C's allocator, and the trampolines and contexts through which C calls a Rust closure
  back; and
- `mod ffi_export { use super::*; … }`: the gateway through which C reaches the module by

receiver already supplies it, and the idiomatic Rust term is preferred over a
transliterated C one. The filled anchor records the C name, so renaming costs no
traceability. Names that cross the language boundary keep their C-derived spelling, as
below.

A C function's raw binding is `sys::<name>`. Its safe wrapper is a free function homed in
the owning module, named by the rules above. When one C function has several valid
ownership contracts, each safe variant has a distinct, descriptive name.

A wrapped C type is the layout-compatible newtype `Foo`, named by the rules above; its
shared and exclusive borrowed handles are `FooRef<'a>` and `FooMut<'a>`, and its sole and
counted owners `FooBox` and `FooArc`. A port keeps these names while what they name
changes, as [`porting-types`](../porting/types/SKILL.md)'s Structs section describes. A typedef that
names a type under another name, which its item lists among its `typedefs`, is a
`pub type` alias of the type's Rust form.

named after the site that declares it, its holder's name followed by its own and `Fn`: a
field's `<Struct><Field>Fn`, a parameter's `<Function><Param>Fn`, a return's
`<Function>ReturnFn` and a global's `<Global>Fn`.

### 1.3 Shims

A callable macro shim is `crustify_<NAME>`.

Each ported module has one raw ABI gateway, its `ffi_export` region, as
[Unsafe regions](#21-unsafe-regions) describes, whose exports use `#[unsafe(no_mangle)] extern "C"` under the bare C names: the
module's functions and globals that C outside the module references, another module's TU
or a C test or executable that stays, the `static inline` functions its headers define
included. The exports serve that C, which reaches the module through them once it has
switched. A function or global only the module's own C references is not exported: that
C leaves the build with the module at its switch, and its callers are Rust from then
on; nor are static functions and static globals, which nothing outside their TU reaches.

target's own remaining C alone, and that API is a layer of its own over the native Rust API,

<!-- TODO: that layer, a C-compatible ABI over the ported public API, is not specified
yet. Until it is, a C consumer outside the target does not survive a port. -->

content.content: --- name: ffibox description: "The library the campaign's Rust holds C memory through, in both directions: owners, handles, lifecycle policies, status conventions, callbacks and exports. Read before writing any wrapper, owner, lifecycle strategy, callable type or export, when judging a crate for adoption, and when testing or reviewing one." --- # ffibox ffibox is the library a campaign's Rust expresses C's ownership and lifetime conventions through, in both directions: memory C allocates, frees, copies, refcounts or locks, held from Rust behind a safe API, and memory Rust owns that C holds, calls or reads. Its primitives stand in for raw pointers and hand-written `Drop` impls wherever C aliases a value; what C does not alias is plain Rust. Its `README.md` is read in full before the first wrapper is written, and each section below names the documents under its `docs/` that its stage reads, also in full. Which primitive serves which C declaration, and how each is built, is those documents'. A representation ffibox cannot express is hand-written, as its `docs/hand-written.md` describes, with the same seam and safety-comment discipline. Its goals and non-goals, `docs/goals.md`, are what a change to ffibox is judged against, as [`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md) describes. What follows is how ffibox serves each stage: each section names the skill and section it adds to, and states only what ffibox adds there. ## Planning ### Dependencies › Adopted crates A candidate crate's soundness is read against the hazards `docs/goals.md`'s G9 lists, each of which ffibox excludes from the campaign's own bindings: the crate qualifies where its safe API excludes them too, by whatever means it uses. ## Binding workflow ### Binding workflow › Rust tree The workspace depends on ffibox by path, on the checkout the host provides, which is on the campaign's working branch of it, `ffibox = { path = "/crustify-rs/ffibox" }` in Crustify's image, so that each run records its revision among its task's `revisions`. The path is the checkout's canonical one, with no symbolic link on it, and a `[patch]` that redirects another source of ffibox names the same: compile-fail snapshots normalize a path dependency only where the compiler's paths match the dependency's canonical directory. ## Binding and porting Binding reads `docs/ownership.md`, `docs/borrows.md`, `docs/patterns.md`, `docs/vtables.md` and `docs/hand-written.md`; porting reads `docs/outbound.md` too. ### Binding types A type that stays interoperable with C is bound through ffibox's primitives wherever they apply, as `docs/ownership.md` and `docs/borrows.md` walk from its C declaration to them. ### Binding types › Safe layout While a type keeps its C layout, `define_ctype!` mints `Foo`, `FooRef<'a>` and `FooMut<'a>`, and its owners are aliases of ffibox's owners over the policy that names its lifecycle routines: `pub type FooBox = CBox;`, and `CArc` for `FooArc`. A value held inline that disposes its resources on drop is a `CVal`. ### Binding symbols › Functions A C routine's status convention becomes a `Result` through `status`, an object returned through an out-parameter a return value through `from_c_out` or `from_raw_out`, and C's iteration conventions iterators, as `docs/patterns.md` maps them. ### Binding symbols › Function pointers A function pointer's callable type is a `CCallback`, where C holds it for a call or a borrow, or a `CCallbackBox`, where C keeps it until it releases its context. Its Rust half is a closure, a `CClosure` or a `CPayload`, which C reaches through its trampoline; its C half is a C function with its context, a `CFn` or a `CFnBox`, which Rust calls, built only inside the crate through its `unsafe` constructor. A trampoline is the panic barrier, `callback::barrier`, which also guards an export's body. A struct of function pointers a library calls into, implemented by a Rust trait, is a `CTable` whose slots `impl_cvtable!` mints, over the binding's own `unsafe impl CVtable`, as `docs/vtables.md` describes; a table C implements is held as any other C object. A family of hooks that carries no context is trampolines over `callback::barrier`, not a table. ### Binding symbols › Lifecycle strategies Each lifecycle is held by the owner `docs/ownership.md` chooses for its shape, over the policy that names its routines; a policy with state, such as an allocator context, is held by `CBoxState`. # ffibox

Generic smart pointers and traits for building safe Rust wrappers over C
types and pointers, in both directions: memory C owns, held from Rust, and
memory Rust owns that C holds, calls or reads. Designed for arbitrary
user-space C interop, including the case where you need direct field access
and a C-ABI-compatible layout (porting C internals to Rust in place), not just
opaque-handle wrapping.

## Why

Wrapping a C API in Rust means re-homing C's ownership and lifecycle
conventions into RAII. The recurring shapes:

- A C-allocated object with a destructor (`free`), and maybe a copy (`dup`).
- A constructor or allocator (`foo_alloc`, `malloc`, `calloc`) whose result
  must be released by its paired free.
- A refcounted object shared by several holders (`up_ref` / `unref`), maybe
  with a C lock over the state they mutate.
- Types with multiple or runtime-conditional destructors.
- A by-value struct whose teardown disposes its fields but not the struct.
- An owned length-aware buffer or NUL-terminated `char *` with a C destructor.
- A type-erased `void *` that stays opaque end to end.

Each shape gets one owner type, generic over a **policy** — a type you declare
that names the C routines. `impl_cdrop!` and its siblings bind a C routine to a
policy; a type alias names the pair: `pub type FooBox = CBox<Foo, FooFree>;`.

## Mental model in one paragraph

No reference to C-owned memory is formed while anything may write or free it:
objects are reached through handles, and only a run of bytes nothing writes
while it is lent is a `&CStr` or `&[u8]`. Each C type gets a layout type
`Foo` (`#[repr(transparent)]` over `ffi::foo`; `Foo<'r>` when the C object
borrows its parent) and two borrowed handles, `FooRef<'a>` / `FooMut<'a>`,
each one pointer wide and carrying the getters and setters; field access projects a raw pointer out of the handle. Ownership
comes in three shapes: `CBox<Foo, P>` is the sole owner of an object behind a
pointer and releases it through the policy `P`; `CArc<Foo, P>` is one of
several counted references and hands out the shared handle, the exclusive one
only when the count proves it sole, and — for an object with a C lock — a
`CGuard` whose `FooLocked<'a>` handle reaches the state that lock protects; and
`CVal<Foo, P>` holds the object inline and disposes its resources on drop.
A policy that also constructs gives `CBox` and `CArc` safe constructors that
allocate through it, so a safely built owner is always freed by the routine
paired with its allocator.
Strings, buffers and borrowed runs get their own types; a buffer drops its
elements, so a `foo **` of owned objects releases each one.

The other direction uses the same terms. `RustAlloc` is the policy over Rust's
allocator, so an object Rust allocates is held as one C allocated, and
`CAllocator` is a C allocation family as the standard `Allocator`, so a
`Box` or `Vec` holds memory C frees; `CClosure`
and `CPayload` put a Rust closure behind a C function pointer and its
context, for one call or until C releases it; `CFn` and `CFnBox` hold a C
function and its context that Rust calls, and `CCallback` and `CCallbackBox`
either half; `CTable` holds Rust state behind a C table of function
pointers C calls into, its slots minted by `impl_cvtable!` from a trait the
Rust side implements; the `export_*!` macros offer a policy to C as the
routine it calls, with the owner and handle types in its signature.
[docs/ownership.md](docs/ownership.md) lists the owners and the policies;
[docs/borrows.md](docs/borrows.md) lists the handles. Each walks from a C
declaration to the type it wants.

## Install

```toml
[dependencies]
ffibox = "0.1"
```

ffibox needs Rust 1.100 or later (`rust-version` in `Cargo.toml`), the first
release with the standard `Allocator` interface, which `CAllocator` implements
over a C allocation family.

ffibox is `#![no_std]`. The `std` feature (on by default) selects
`std::process::abort` for the unrecoverable-failure path (`Clone` or
`make_mut` when the C copy or up_ref fails), where without it that path is a
double-panic, and lets `CClosure`, `CTable`'s slots and `callback::barrier`
catch a panic before it reaches C. The `alloc` feature, which `std` enables,
adds `RustAlloc`, `CPayload`, `CCallbackBox` and `CTable`, which allocate
through Rust's global allocator, and the conversions between ffibox's owners
and `Box` / `Vec`; nothing else allocates but through a policy the consumer
chose, as `CAllocator` allocates through its family.

```toml
[dependencies]
ffibox = { version = "0.1", default-features = false }
```

## Documentation

Every wrapper answers one question first: **does dropping the Rust value
release the object?** This is about who *releases* the object, not who
allocated it — a `CBox` usually points at memory C allocated.

- **Yes** — it is owned → [docs/ownership.md](docs/ownership.md)
- **No** — C, or a parent object, releases it → [docs/borrows.md](docs/borrows.md)

When it is Rust's memory that C holds, calls or reads →
[docs/outbound.md](docs/outbound.md).

| [examples.md](docs/examples.md) | eight self-contained wrappers, each compiled as a doctest |
| [ownership.md](docs/ownership.md) | `CBox`, `CBoxState`, `CVal`, `CStrBox`, `CVec`, `CArc`; the lifecycle policies; picking an owner and a policy; `Box` and `Vec` over a C allocator (`CAllocator`) |
| [borrows.md](docs/borrows.md) | `Foo`, `FooRef`, `FooMut`, `FooLocked`, `CGuard`, `CGuardedRef`, `CSlice`, `CSliceMut`, `CNullTerminated`; where the accessors live; the seam traits |
| [outbound.md](docs/outbound.md) | Rust's side: `RustAlloc`, the callbacks (`CClosure`, `CPayload`, `CFn`, `CFnBox`, `CCallback`, `CCallbackBox`), C tables (`CTable`), out-parameters, the panic barrier, the `export_*!` macros |
| [vtables.md](docs/vtables.md) | C tables of function pointers implemented in Rust: `CTable`, `impl_cvtable!`, their receivers, re-entry, panics and release, and the design |
| [patterns.md](docs/patterns.md) | C's iteration, error and callback conventions as Rust's iterators, `Result` and closures |
| [hand-written.md](docs/hand-written.md) | the wrappers `define_ctype!` cannot express (a layout type generic over a type), and the owners no policy expresses |

Upgrading? [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md) says what each release changes, and
how to migrate code that still compiles but behaves differently.

# C tables implemented in Rust

A C library often takes a **table**: a struct of function pointers it calls
into, each slot passed a pointer to the table itself, which the implementer
embeds at the start of a larger allocation holding its own state. libgit2's
`git_config_backend`, `git_odb_backend` and `git_writestream` are such tables;
so is any "C inheritance" base struct with a `free` slot. Rust implements one

| an object returned through an out-parameter | a return value | `CBox::from_c_out`, `CStrBox::from_raw_out` |
| a `foreach(callback, context)` visitor | a closure | `CClosure` |
| a callback the library keeps | a boxed closure | `CPayload` |


# Borrows

A borrow is a handle over an object something else releases — C, or a parent
object. It is one pointer wide, carries a lifetime, and is never a Rust
reference to the C object itself.

For the owning side — values whose drop releases the object — see
[ownership.md](ownership.md).

## The handles

| Scope | Type | From | Role |
|-------|------|------|------|
| per C type | `Foo` | `define_ctype!` | the layout, the C struct's size: `#[repr(transparent)]` over `ffi::foo`, embeds by value in a `#[repr(C)]` mirror, and is what a `CBox` points at. Never referenced over C-owned memory. Also the value itself when it owns no resources (a rational `{ num, den }`). |
| | `FooRef<'a>` | `define_ctype!` | shared borrow, one pointer wide, `Copy`; the getters |
| | `FooMut<'a>` | `define_ctype!` | exclusive borrow, move-only; the setters, and the getters through `as_ref()` |
| per C lock | `FooLocked<'a>` | `impl_cguarded!` | exclusive borrow under the C lock, move-only; getters and setters for the state the lock protects, the unlocked getters through `as_ref()` |
| lock | `CGuard<'a, Foo>` | ffibox | a held C lock, unlocking on drop — `MutexGuard`; `as_locked()` → `FooLocked<'_>`, `as_ref()` → `FooRef<'_>` |
| guarded borrow | `CGuardedRef<'a, Foo>` | ffibox | an object under one lock covering all of it (`CGuardedAll`), never released — typically a C global (`'static`); only `lock()`, whose `as_locked()` is `FooMut` — `&Mutex<_>` |
| views | `CSlice<'a, T>` / `CSliceMut<'a, T>` | ffibox | any borrowed run of elements — a buffer's, a struct field's, a getter's — as handles or copies, never a `&[T]`; only a run of plain values nothing writes while it is lent is a `&[T]` instead, as [Choosing a borrow](#choosing-a-borrow) describes |
| | `CNullTerminated<'a, T>` | ffibox | a NULL-terminated array of pointers (`char **`, `foo **`), iterated as `&CStr`s or `FooRef`s |

A layout type that carries a lifetime, over a C object that keeps a pointer
to its parent, is `define_ctype!`'s too: `define_ctype!(Blob<'r>, BlobRef,
BlobMut, ffi::blob, phantom = &'r Repo)` gives `Blob<'r>`, `BlobRef<'a, 'r>`
and `BlobMut<'a, 'r>`, the marker deciding how `Blob` varies in `'r`. A
wrapper that needs type parameters (derived sub-types over a generic field) is
written by hand against the same contract — see
[Under the hood](hand-written.md). Its policies still come from the macros
where they take the type.

## Conventions

- **Accessors live on the handles.** Getters on `FooRef<'a>` taking `&self`,
  setters on `FooMut<'a>` taking `&mut self`; `FooMut` reaches the getters with
  `as_ref()`, so they are written once. Both project a raw pointer out of the
  handle and read or write through `addr_of!` / `addr_of_mut!`.
- **Every holder reaches the handles the same way:** `as_ref()` / `as_mut()` on
  `Foo`, `CBox`, `CBoxState`, `CVal` and `FooMut` itself (where `as_mut()` is
  the reborrow `&mut` gets implicitly: `helper(m.as_mut())` keeps `m`);
  `as_ref()` on `CArc`, whose exclusive handle comes only from `get_mut()` /
  `make_mut()`; `as_ref()` / `as_locked()` on a `CGuard` and on `FooLocked` (where
  `as_locked()` reborrows). `CSliceMut` reborrows the same
  way, and splits and sub-ranges like `&mut [T]`. Never `Deref`:
  `Deref::Target` cannot name a lifetime taken from `&self`, and since `FooRef`
  is `Copy`, a `Deref<Target = FooRef<'a>>` on `FooMut` would let safe code copy
  a shared handle out while keeping the exclusive one.
- **No reference covers C memory anything may write.** `&FooRef` covers one pointer of Rust stack,
  never the object. The one place a reference covers a C struct's bytes is
  `Foo::as_ref` / `as_mut` on a value Rust holds inline. A run of bytes an
  object lends, a NUL string or a counted run, is lent as `&CStr` or `&[u8]`
  only while nothing writes it, as [Choosing a borrow](#choosing-a-borrow)
  describes; otherwise it is a `CSlice`.
- **The handles' seams are traits the macros implement:** `CRefSeam` on
  `FooRef` (`from_ptr`, `as_ptr` and the `void *` pair), `CMutSeam` on `FooMut`
  (`from_ptr`, `as_mut_ptr` and the `void *` pair) and `CLockedSeam` on
  `FooLocked` (`as_mut_ptr` alone). Import them wherever the seam is used, in
  the crate that invokes `define_ctype!` or in any other that holds its
  handles. Their methods are provided once, by ffibox, so the wrapper crate
  defines no raw-pointer method of its own for them. The inbound half is also
  on `CCell` (`ref_from_ptr`, `mut_from_ptr` and the `void *` twins), so
  generic code over `T: CCell` can borrow a pointer C gives it; those are
  `unsafe`, and the handles' `from_ptr` forward to them. Adopting ownership is
  a different verb on a different type — see
  [ownership.md](ownership.md#conventions).

## Choosing a borrow

Reached when dropping the Rust value does *not* release the object. When it
does, the answer is an owner — see
[ownership.md](ownership.md#choosing-an-owner-what-shape-is-the-owned-thing).

- **No — C, or a parent object, releases it.** Borrow it:
  - one object → `FooRef<'a>` / `FooMut<'a>`, its lifetime tied to whatever
    keeps it alive (a parent's handle, the call);
  - a run of elements → `CSlice<'a, T>` / `CSliceMut<'a, T>`;
  - a counted run of immutable bytes an object lends, `const uint8_t *data`
    with its `size_t len` (from a getter pair, or two fields) → `&'a [u8]`
    from `core::slice::from_raw_parts`, tied to the shared handle's `'a`, as a
    NUL string is a `&CStr`. A run of other `CPlainElem` values is the same
    `&'a [T]`. The SAFETY comment shows, from C's contract, that:
    - nothing writes, moves or frees the bytes while the shared handle lives:
      no routine reachable through a `FooRef` writes, grows or reallocates
      them (not one on `FooRef`, not one on a `FooLocked` taken beside it, not
      another thread's, if `Foo` is `Sync`); a write reachable only through
      `FooMut` is excluded by the borrow;
    - they live as long as the object does, freed with it or with a parent the
      lifetime covers, not by the next call that refills a shared buffer; and
    - `data` addresses `len` initialised bytes in one allocation. A NULL or
      empty run returns `&[]` without the call, since `from_raw_parts` takes
      no NULL even for a length of 0.

    Where any of these fails, as for a cache, a buffer the library refills or
    reallocates behind a `const` pointer, or state another thread writes, the
    run is a `CSlice<'a, u8>` built with `CSlice::from_raw_parts`, which forms
    no reference: `elems`, `copy_to_slice` and `to_cvec` copy the bytes out.
    The element type does not decide between the two, since a `u8` is plain
    either way: who may write the bytes does. A caller that keeps the bytes
    past the object's borrow takes an owned copy;
  - a NULL-terminated array of pointers → `CNullTerminated<'a, T>`, an
    `Iterator` of the elements' borrows; a `count` + `get(i)` pair or a
    `->next` chain is `(0..n).map(get)` or `iter::successors` over the safe
    getter;
  - an object every access reaches under one lock covering all of it —
    typically a C global and the C lock protecting it → `CGuardedRef<'a, Foo>`,
    `'static` for a global, with `impl_cguarded!(Foo, all, …)`;
  - a NUL string → `&CStr` / `&str` / `&[u8]` tied to the owner's borrow,
    on the terms of a counted byte run above;
  - an out-parameter slot → `&'a mut MaybeUninit<T>` from
    `ptr.cast::<MaybeUninit<T>>().as_mut()`; no ffibox type;
  - a `void *` → if it is really a `ffi::foo`, erase a `FooRef` with
    `as_void_ptr` and recover it with `from_void_ptr` (generically,
    `T::ref_from_void_ptr` / `T::mut_from_void_ptr` for `T: CCell`); if it is a
    cookie never looked inside, pass the raw `*mut c_void` through unchanged.

  A borrow that must outlive its parent's scope (stored next to the parent,
  sent to a thread) cannot be expressed as a lifetime; copy the child into an
  owned object instead.
# Hand-written wrappers

Only a wrapper `define_ctype!` cannot express — a layout type generic over a
type — needs this layer, and so does an owner no policy expresses:
[an array freed by one routine](#an-array-freed-by-one-routine) that does
more than free its elements and itself. A layout type that carries only
lifetimes is not hand-written: `define_ctype!` declares it,
`define_ctype!(Blob<'r>, BlobRef, BlobMut, ffi::blob, phantom = &'r Repo)`,
as [examples.md](examples.md#a-layout-type-with-a-lifetime--define_ctype-with-phantom)
shows. One already written by hand is the same layout, and moves to the macro
when its module is next touched, or stays.

A C table a library calls into and Rust implements (a backend, a stream:
a struct of function pointers, each passed the table) is not hand-written
either: `CTable` lays it out with its state, recovers the state in each slot,
guards re-entry, puts each slot behind the panic barrier and releases it once,
and `impl_cvtable!` mints the slots, as [vtables.md](vtables.md) describes.
Only a slot the macro cannot express is written by hand, as an
`unsafe extern "C" fn` whose body is `CTable::enter`, in a hand-written
`CSlots<S>` impl beside an `unsafe impl CVtable<S>`.

What is hand-written for such a wrapper is the layout type, its handles and
their seams, against the items below. Its policies are not, unless no macro
takes them:

- **A layout type generic over a type** (`Stack<T, S>`) has no elided form,
  so each of its policies is an `unsafe impl<T, S>` by hand.
- **A hand-written layout type with a lifetime** takes every policy macro, as
  a `define_ctype!` one does: `impl_cdrop!(BlobFree, Blob<'_>, ffi::blob_free)`
  implements `CDrop<Blob<'r>>` for every `'r`, and `impl_cdupclone!` and
  `impl_cguarded!` name the lifetime, `<'r> BlobFree, Blob<'r>`, as
  [ownership.md](ownership.md#policies--what-teardown-means) explains.
- **A routine of another shape** (a slot, an out-parameter, extra arguments)
  is no reason to hand-write a policy: a private `unsafe fn` adapter passed to
  the macro gives it the shape the macro calls, as
  [ownership.md](ownership.md#policies--what-teardown-means) describes.

| Item | Role | Source |
|------|------|--------|
| `CCell` | the linking trait: `type C` (the FFI type), `type Ref<'a>`, `type Mut<'a>`, and the provided, `unsafe` inbound seam (`ref_from_ptr`, `mut_from_ptr` and their `void *` twins). Its `unsafe impl` promises that `Self` is layout-compatible with `C`, and that `Ref` / `Mut` are `#[repr(transparent)]` over `CBorrowedPtr<'a, Self>` with no `Drop`, and `Mut` invariant in `Self` (a `PhantomData<&'a mut Self>` field) — ffibox builds handles from that layout, and checks their size at compile time. | `src/traits.rs` |
| `CRefSeam` / `CMutSeam` / `CLockedSeam` | the handles' seams, every method provided from the layout `CCell` (or `CGuarded`) guarantees: implement them on hand-written handles with `type Cell = Foo;`, as the macros do, or the handles have no `as_ptr` / `as_mut_ptr`. | `src/traits.rs` |
| `CBorrowedPtr<'a, T>` | what every handle wraps: one pointer tagged with the borrow's lifetime, `Copy` and covariant like `&'a T`. | `src/refs.rs` |
| `CPlainElem` | marker for plain-data elements: every bit pattern is a valid value and there is no C-side identity. It admits `&[T]` from a `CVec`, as a `CSliceElem` (a wrapped C type implements `CCell` instead, so `&[Foo]` does not typecheck), and makes copies read out of memory C keeps writing sound. Not the same as initialized: an unfilled buffer is `CVec<MaybeUninit<T>, _>` until `assume_init`. | `src/traits.rs` |
| `CSliceElem` | elements a `CVec` hands out as `&[T]` / `&mut [T]`: every `CPlainElem`, and the owners — `CBox`, `CArc` and `CStrBox`, bare or in an `Option`, and `CVal` — whose references cover a Rust value, never C memory. A hand-written owner implements it on the same terms. | `src/traits.rs` |

**Layout.** `CBox`, `CArc` and `CStrBox` are `#[repr(transparent)]` over their
pointer, and their policy is stateless, held in no bytes: `Option<CBox<Foo, P>>`
is a `ffi::foo *`, NULL for `None`, as Rust guarantees for `Option<NonNull<_>>`.
So it takes a raw pointer's place in a `#[repr(C)]` struct, a `foo **` buffer
and an `extern "C"` signature alike. A policy with state fails to build in
them; it is held by `CBoxState<Foo, P>`, `#[repr(C)]` over `{ptr, policy}`,
which crosses as a raw pointer. `CVal<Foo, P>` is the size of `Foo` under a
stateless policy; a buffer is pointer + length, the pointer NULL when empty,
as C's `{ T *ptr; size_t len; }`.

## An array freed by one routine

A `CVec` releases an array of owners element by element, then frees the
buffer through `CLenDrop`, which frees the buffer only (see
[ownership.md](ownership.md#choosing-an-owner-what-shape-is-the-owned-thing)).
That covers a C routine whose body is only those frees. One that does more
— takes a lock, updates a count, or releases an element other than by
freeing it — is not a policy: the wrapper writes the owner itself, as `CVec`
is written:

- private fields, the pointer and the length, adopted by an `unsafe`
  constructor whose contract is the routine's: the array is one the routine
  frees, and its non-null elements are distinct allocations it owns;
- a `Drop` that calls the routine once, with both;
- the elements handed out as borrows tied to `&self` — `FooRef<'_>` through
  `CRefSeam::from_ptr`, `&CStr`, a `CSlice` of the pointers, which copies
  them out — never as `&mut` to a slot, through which safe code would store
  a pointer, or NULL, that the routine then frees.

A C table a library calls into and Rust implements (a backend, a stream:
a struct of function pointers, each passed the table) is not hand-written
either: `CTable` lays it out with its state, recovers the state in each slot,
guards re-entry, puts each slot behind the panic barrier and releases it once,
and `impl_cvtable!` mints the slots, as [vtables.md](vtables.md) describes.
Only a slot the macro cannot express is written by hand, as an
`unsafe extern "C" fn` whose body is `CTable::enter`, in a hand-written
`CSlots<S>` impl beside an `unsafe impl CVtable<S>`.

What is hand-written for such a wrapper is the layout type, its handles and
their seams, against the items below. Its policies are not, unless no macro
takes them:

- **A layout type generic over a type** (`Stack<T, S>`) has no elided form,
  so each of its policies is an `unsafe impl<T, S>` by hand.
- **A hand-written layout type with a lifetime** takes every policy macro, as
  a `define_ctype!` one does: `impl_cdrop!(BlobFree, Blob<'_>, ffi::blob_free)`
  implements `CDrop<Blob<'r>>` for every `'r`, and `impl_cdupclone!` and
  `impl_cguarded!` name the lifetime, `<'r> BlobFree, Blob<'r>`, as
  [ownership.md](ownership.md#policies--what-teardown-means) explains.
- **A routine of another shape** (a slot, an out-parameter, extra arguments)
  is no reason to hand-write a policy: a private `unsafe fn` adapter passed to
  the macro gives it the shape the macro calls, as
  [ownership.md](ownership.md#policies--what-teardown-means) describes.

| Item | Role | Source |
|------|------|--------|
| `CCell` | the linking trait: `type C` (the FFI type), `type Ref<'a>`, `type Mut<'a>`, and the provided, `unsafe` inbound seam (`ref_from_ptr`, `mut_from_ptr` and their `void *` twins). Its `unsafe impl` promises that `Self` is layout-compatible with `C`, and that `Ref` / `Mut` are `#[repr(transparent)]` over `CBorrowedPtr<'a, Self>` with no `Drop`, and `Mut` invariant in `Self` (a `PhantomData<&'a mut Self>` field) — ffibox builds handles from that layout, and checks their size at compile time. | `src/traits.rs` |
| `CRefSeam` / `CMutSeam` / `CLockedSeam` | the handles' seams, every method provided from the layout `CCell` (or `CGuarded`) guarantees: implement them on hand-written handles with `type Cell = Foo;`, as the macros do, or the handles have no `as_ptr` / `as_mut_ptr`. | `src/traits.rs` |
| `CBorrowedPtr<'a, T>` | what every handle wraps: one pointer tagged with the borrow's lifetime, `Copy` and covariant like `&'a T`. | `src/refs.rs` |
| `CPlainElem` | marker for plain-data elements: every bit pattern is a valid value and there is no C-side identity. It admits `&[T]` from a `CVec`, as a `CSliceElem` (a wrapped C type implements `CCell` instead, so `&[Foo]` does not typecheck), and makes copies read out of memory C keeps writing sound. Not the same as initialized: an unfilled buffer is `CVec<MaybeUninit<T>, _>` until `assume_init`. | `src/traits.rs` |
| `CSliceElem` | elements a `CVec` hands out as `&[T]` / `&mut [T]`: every `CPlainElem`, and the owners — `CBox`, `CArc` and `CStrBox`, bare or in an `Option`, and `CVal` — whose references cover a Rust value, never C memory. A hand-written owner implements it on the same terms. | `src/traits.rs` |

**Layout.** `CBox`, `CArc` and `CStrBox` are `#[repr(transparent)]` over their
pointer, and their policy is stateless, held in no bytes: `Option<CBox<Foo, P>>`
is a `ffi::foo *`, NULL for `None`, as Rust guarantees for `Option<NonNull<_>>`.
So it takes a raw pointer's place in a `#[repr(C)]` struct, a `foo **` buffer
and an `extern "C"` signature alike. A policy with state fails to build in
them; it is held by `CBoxState<Foo, P>`, `#[repr(C)]` over `{ptr, policy}`,
which crosses as a raw pointer. `CVal<Foo, P>` is the size of `Foo` under a
stateless policy; a buffer is pointer + length, the pointer NULL when empty,
as C's `{ T *ptr; size_t len; }`.

## An array freed by one routine

A `CVec` releases an array of owners element by element, then frees the
buffer through `CLenDrop`, which frees the buffer only (see
[ownership.md](ownership.md#choosing-an-owner-what-shape-is-the-owned-thing)).
That covers a C routine whose body is only those frees. One that does more
— takes a lock, updates a count, or releases an element other than by
freeing it — is not a policy: the wrapper writes the owner itself, as `CVec`
is written:

- private fields, the pointer and the length, adopted by an `unsafe`
  constructor whose contract is the routine's: the array is one the routine
  frees, and its non-null elements are distinct allocations it owns;
- a `Drop` that calls the routine once, with both;
- the elements handed out as borrows tied to `&self` — `FooRef<'_>` through
  `CRefSeam::from_ptr`, `&CStr`, a `CSlice` of the pointers, which copies
  them out — never as `&mut` to a slot, through which safe code would store
  a pointer, or NULL, that the routine then frees.

---
name: wavefront
description: "Deterministic queries and dependency-ordered plans over the C codebase, the first resort for any question about it: entities, uses, dependencies, pointers, lifecycles, T3 cast tables. Read before querying the C codebase, before planning, decomposing or scheduling, before analysing or binding an item, when packing wrap batches, when reviewing pointer findings or lifecycles, and before changing wavefront itself."
---

# wavefront

Wavefront answers deterministic queries about a C codebase, its entities, their uses and
dependencies, their pointers and lifecycles, and generates dependency-ordered wave plans
over it.

It is the first resort for any question about the C codebase: an entity's definition,
fields or signature, its users, callers and casts, what it depends on, and the pointer
findings and lifecycle roles submitted on it are queried rather than searched for in the
source, so that each answer covers every site the traced build compiles, and every query
of one fact gets one answer. The source is read where wavefront records nothing, to read a
body, and to judge what wavefront records.

Its `README.md` and `--help` are read in full before its first command, and each section
below names the documents under its `docs/` that its stage reads, also in full. How
wavefront scopes, orders and batches, what its configuration, tables and records hold, and
what each query returns are those documents', and are not restated here. Its goals and
non-goals, `docs/goals.md`, are what a change to wavefront is judged against, as
[`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md) describes.

## Campaign state

Wavefront's repo root is the C root: it is passed `<workdir>/c`, so that every path it
reads and reports is relative to the C root, as the plan records them. Its state sits
under `crustify/wavefront/`, which the configuration names as its `state_dir`,
`../crustify/wavefront`:

- `codeql/`, the CodeQL database and its T1/T2 tables, and `.cache`, both gitignored;
- `configs/wavefront-config.json`, the campaign's configuration, which every query of the
  bindings and reviews resolves through, with `"t3_dir": "t3"`;
- `t3/`, the T3 tables, one campaign-wide pair; and
- `ownership-store.json`, the findings submitted to it through the CLI. A finding
  submitted once is queried again rather than re-derived.

The configuration's `modules` hold one record per module of `modules.json`, named
`<link-unit>/<name>`, with ` (foundational)` after a foundational module's name.

What follows is how wavefront serves each stage: each section names the skill and section
it adds to, and states only what wavefront adds there.

## Batches

### Versioning › Lifecycle › Batches

The CodeQL database and tables under `crustify/wavefront/codeql/`, and wavefront's
`.cache`, are gitignored state every batch needs: they are symlinked into each batch's
worktree once it is forked.

## Binding and porting

Binding and porting read `docs/pointer-properties.md`, `docs/type-lifecycle.md`,
`docs/artifacts/findings.md` and `docs/artifacts/t3.md`.

### Analysis

An item's analysis queries the campaign's configuration, and its findings are submitted
to the ownership store. A type-erased parameter or field is looked up in the T3 tables before it
is bound, and the binding names the type a row gives it rather than a raw pointer. The
instances of a type generator share one generic, with per-instance aliases.

### Binding types › Surface

A type's lifecycle primitives are identified as `docs/type-lifecycle.md` describes, and
submitted to the ownership store.

### Binding symbols › Function pointers

A function pointer's record and its users are those of wavefront's function-pointer query,
named as `docs/graph.md`'s Nodes section names it, and the sites of one written inline,
and what reaches them, are as `docs/batching.md`'s Release points section describes.
<!-- TODO: no query lists an inline function pointer's sites yet: they are read from the
table that section names. -->

### Binding symbols › Lifecycle strategies

Each foundational item's lifecycle role is in the ownership store, where planning
submitted it, and is queried for every item of the batch. A role that the item's body
contradicts is corrected in the ownership store, and the correction named in the batch's commit
message.

### Porting types

A ported type's lifecycle primitives are identified as `docs/type-lifecycle.md`
describes, and submitted to the ownership store.

## Evolution

A change to wavefront reads its README's Tests section, which names its opt-in CodeQL
tests: a change to a query or a fixture's C runs them, as the `evolution` skill's Changes
section asks of a tool's opt-in tests.

---
name: ffimap
description: "Deterministic counts and sites of a Rust crate's unsafe and FFI surface. Read before a batch lands (its safe-boundary scan and safety-audit cells), before planning an audit's worksets, and when reviewing for unsafety, contracts or UB."
---

# ffimap

ffimap maps a Rust crate's FFI and unsafe surface deterministically: a rustc driver over
HIR and typeck counts unsafe blocks and fns, raw and void pointers by position and
visibility, FFI calls and wrapper use. No model is involved, so two runs over one tree
agree exactly. Its `--help` lists its flags, and its `docs/schema.md`, read in full before
its first scan, its counters and how a report combines them.

It counts what the build compiles of the safe crate itself, and prints one JSON document:

```bash
ffimap <workdir> > <file>.json
```

Every scan names the crate's seams, the functions that hand a value between its wrapper and
its raw form, so that each counter's `of_which.seam` share tells that plumbing apart from
the pointer management a consumer of the safe API faces: ffibox's handle seams `as_ptr`,
`as_mut_ptr`, `as_void_ptr`, `from_ptr` and `from_void_ptr`, the ownership hand-offs
`from_raw_parts`, `into_raw_parts`, `into_raw`, `from_c`, `into_c` and `as_c_ptr`, the adoption of a raw C
value, `from_raw`, and the view of a C object as another, `as_object`. A crate built on
ffibox is scanned with `--ffibox`, and its `-sys` crates are named with `--sys-crates`:

```bash
ffimap <workdir> --ffibox --sys-crates <the -sys crates> --regions ffi_import,ffi_export \
    --seams as_ptr,as_mut_ptr,as_void_ptr,from_ptr,from_void_ptr,from_raw_parts,into_raw_parts,into_raw,from_c,into_c,as_c_ptr,from_raw,as_object \
```
